source.title: Towards Principled Evaluations of Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Control
source.authors: Aleksandar Makelov; Georg Lange; Neel Nanda

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates SAE feature dictionaries with task-specific tests of interpretability, approximation, and control, rather than reproducing the original toy-model superposition method.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses prior work on superposition, but cited results are not recorded. Its own results on supervised dictionaries and SAE features, feature occlusion, and feature over-splitting are included where they bear on the tested versions. Values visible only in figures are not transcribed as numbers.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates SAE dictionaries on GPT-2 Small's IOI task against supervised dictionaries. Its results on approximation, control, interpretability, occlusion and over-splitting bear directly on whether SAE features are the model's units (V5) and on whether SAEs recover sparse features in an LLM (V4). Much of this argues V5 needs qualifying, hence T5 rather than a plain T2 re-test.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add three points. Supervised dictionaries achieve excellent approximation, control and interpretability and serve as skylines. Task-specific SAEs allow sparser edits than full-distribution SAEs, but both fall short of supervised dictionaries. Occlusion and over-splitting are reproduced in toy models, suggesting they may generalize.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates supervised feature dictionaries and SAEs on GPT2-Small’s IOI task; it does not reproduce the original Toy Models of Superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature discovery and SAE control vary with the SAE training distribution and feature magnitude; the authors also report effects of F1 threshold, dictionary size, and regularization during feature evaluations and sweeps.
record.problems: The study covers one language model and one task. The authors did not exhaustively tune SAE hyperparameters in the main experiments; some interpretability results are qualitative, and the F1-based interpretation method has acknowledged limitations.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: No toy-model test of superposition geometry, a sparsity-dependent phase transition, or near-orthogonal overlapping features. The occlusion and over-splitting toys concern SAE learning, not stored superposition.
No test of neuron polysemanticity or of capacity competition.
No test of non-capacity causes of polysemantic neurons.
Only one model and one task, with attention-head activations. There is no neuron-level test of features spreading across many neurons.
Canonicity across models or SAE architectures and completeness beyond the IOI task are not tested.
No comparison of 1-D versus multi-dimensional features. Supervised features are fixed-coefficient vectors by construction.

missing.what: Test 1 sufficiency/necessity: task SAEs approximate significantly worse than supervised dictionaries but not catastrophically; full-distribution SAEs fare notably worse.
Frozen-decoder baseline: random-decoder task SAEs perform much worse than trained task SAEs but on par with full-distribution SAEs in control.

Supervised dictionaries (about 500 features, 64-dim heads, about 3 active per activation) approximate, control and interpret IOI activations well. The authors state this exhibits superposition in a realistic LLM task.
Occlusion toy: in an i.i.d. random-feature toy matching IO/S norms, SAEs find high-norm but not low-norm features at F1 above 0.9. The effect fades at lower F1 thresholds.
Interpretation-aware sufficiency/necessity: keeping or removing features with F1 of at least 0.6 largely preserves or degrades task performance.
SAEs learn decompositions resembling features for small, overlapping subsets of names rather than one feature per name.

record.verdict_notes: V4 and V5 are tested here; V1, V2, V3 and V6 are not. The authors note SAE hyperparameters were not exhaustively tuned in the main experiments, which limits how strongly the V5 limitations generalize. The original source is Toy Models of Superposition; this paper is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test the toy-model claim about sparse features exceeding dimensions, their nearly orthogonal overlapping geometry, or a sparsity-dependent transition and regular geometry.
The paper does not test whether neuron polysemanticity results from competition for capacity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
The paper does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise through mechanisms other than capacity pressure.
The study examines SAE feature interpretation on one task and one model; it does not test whether LLM features generally spread across many neurons.
The study evaluates some interpretability, causal faithfulness, and repeatability properties, but does not establish that SAE features are complete or canonical across models and tasks.
The paper does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multi-dimensional feature representations.

rows.subject: GPT2-Small
rows.operation_detail: Scored task-specific SAE features for interpretations of IOI attributes and compared their qualitative patterns with full-distribution SAE features.
rows.measure: Presence of interpretable SAE features for IOI task attributes
rows.value: The authors report interpretable features for the task; they describe task-specific and full-distribution SAE features as qualitatively similar.
rows.locator: Section 5.2, Correlational evaluation; Appendix Figures 26 and 27
rows.note: The paper reports qualitative feature interpretations, not a single aggregate score.

rows.subject: GPT2-Small
rows.operation_detail: Scored full-distribution SAE features that activate on IOI prompts against task-attribute interpretations.
rows.measure: Presence of interpretable SAE features for IOI task attributes
rows.value: Only a subset of full-distribution SAE features activate on IOI prompts; among those, the authors report a significant amount with high F1 scores and qualitative similarity to task-specific SAE features.
rows.note: The text gives no numerical aggregate for the high-F1 subset.

rows.subject: GPT2-Small
rows.operation_detail: Examined how many SAE features represented the binary Pos attribute.
rows.measure: Number and interpretability of features associated with Pos
rows.value: The Pos attribute was split into many (e.g. ≥ 10) features active on small, mostly non-overlapping subsets of examples, without clear semantic interpretations.
rows.note: The authors caution that this behavior does not necessarily mean the SAE failed.

source_check.locator_found: Section 6.2, lines 1156–1163: binary Pos splits into at least 10 features on small, mostly non-overlapping subsets without clear semantic interpretations.

rows.subject: GPT2-Small
rows.operation_detail: Compared the number of high-F1 IO-name and S-name features across an extensive SAE hyperparameter sweep.
rows.measure: Number of discovered features for IO and S names
rows.value: The sweep often found as many IO features as names in the dataset, while the number of S features never exceeded 22.
rows.note: The authors interpret the imbalance as feature occlusion; supervised IO features had somewhat higher norms than supervised S features.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix A.14, lines 2836–2851; Figure 6: 100,000 training examples, dictionaries up to 8192 features, F1 > 0.5; S-feature count never exceeds 22.

rows.subject: GPT2-Small
rows.operation_detail: Reduced the magnitude of supervised IO features in activations and measured the number of high-F1 IO and S features discovered by an SAE.

conditions.value: IO-feature magnitude reduced by α from 0 to 1

rows.measure: Number of features with F1 score > 0.5 for IO and S names
rows.value: As α increased, the number of IO features decreased and the number of S features increased monotonically.
rows.note: The intervention is on purpose; it provides evidence about magnitude-driven occlusion, not spontaneous feature prevalence.
rows.check: The recorded state 'observed' describes the occlusion manipulation working, not V5. Against V5 the result shows that which attribute the SAE learns depends on feature magnitude rather than causal role, so it is a qualification. Reducing IO magnitude is a deliberate input manipulation for the SAE, not induced model behaviour, so the row is valid.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix A.14, lines 2912–2921; Figure 6 right: subtracting α times the supervised IO feature, α from 0 to 1, decreases IO-feature counts and increases S-feature counts; dictionary size 1024, regularization coefficient 0.2.

rows.subject: toy model (Gaussian-mixture SAE)
rows.size_stated: 100 dimensions; SAE with m = 1,000 hidden features
rows.operation_detail: Compared the loss of an idealized two-feature SAE with a randomized many-feature SAE on a uniform mixture of two isotropic Gaussian variables.

conditions.value: uniform mixture of two standard multivariate Gaussians
grid of λ values; plotted range cut off near λ ≈ 7

rows.baseline: Best loss of the idealized two-feature SAE class
rows.value: The randomized many-feature construction was competitive with or better than the idealized two-feature solution across the examined λ values; the authors report that empirically trained many-feature SAEs reliably learned solutions with many active features.
rows.uncertainty: The plotted comparison is described as an approximate upper bound for the many-feature class and an approximate best loss for the ideal class.
rows.note: The authors use this toy result to show that SAE training can favor many features over an intuitive two-feature decomposition.
rows.check: The recorded 'observed' describes over-splitting occurring. Against V5, the natural 2-feature decomposition is not the SAE loss optimum; many-feature solutions match or beat it at every lambda in the toy. Subject is a synthetic toy SAE, not the LLM.

source_check.locator_found: Section 6.2, lines 1169–1175; Appendix A.15 and Figure 14, lines 2979–3060: d = 100, mean norm 2, randomized SAE with m = 1000; approximate loss comparison across λ.

rows.subject: GPT2-Small
rows.operation_detail: Tested whether highly interpretable SAE features were causally faithful and complete using counterfactual feature patching.
rows.measure: Faithfulness and completeness of interpreted features in the causal evaluation
rows.value: At F1 threshold 0.6, the authors report that features were faithful and complete to a high degree.
rows.note: The result is qualitative; the paper does not give a numerical score here.
rows.check: The text says features are faithful and complete 'to a high degree' at F1 0.6. That is full, not partial. The text is from task-SAE interpretations on name mover outputs.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix A.13, lines 2776–2797; repeated in Appendix A.16, lines 3075–3097: name-mover-output patching reports high faithfulness and completeness at F1 threshold 0.6.

rows.subject: GPT2-Small
rows.operation_detail: Repeated the causal feature-interpretation evaluation at higher F1 thresholds.
rows.value: The faithfulness metric significantly decreased at thresholds 0.7 and 0.8.
rows.uncertainty: The authors describe the decrease as significant; no p-value is stated.
rows.note: The authors also report that fixing only features with F1 > 0.8 could preserve the base prompt’s predicted output in the described completeness test.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix A.13, lines 2792–2797; Appendix A.16, lines 3091–3097: faithfulness significantly decreases at thresholds 0.7 and 0.8 relative to 0.6.

rows.subject: GPT2-Small
rows.operation_detail: Edited task attributes using active SAE features and compared with supervised feature edits.

conditions.value: Pos; to a small extent IO

rows.measure: Agreement of edited model predictions with ground-truth counterfactual edits and magnitude of edits
rows.baseline: Corresponding supervised feature edits; no-intervention outcome also shown
rows.value: The authors report that task SAEs can edit Pos and, to a small extent, IO, but require more features than supervised dictionaries; successful edits have higher magnitude than corresponding supervised edits.
rows.uncertainty: The text says S-attribute results are unclear in many locations because no-intervention performance is within the margin of error.
rows.note: The text specifically reports failure of SAE features for S edits in the queries of name mover heads.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5.2, Test 2, lines 771–833; Figures 3 and 4: task SAEs edit Pos and weakly IO using 2, 4 or 6 features, with larger edits than supervised dictionaries; S editing fails in name-mover queries.

rows.subject: GPT2-Small
rows.operation_detail: Edited task attributes using full-distribution SAE features.
rows.measure: Sparse controllability of IOI attributes and magnitude of edits
rows.value: The authors report that a significantly larger number of features was often required for statistically significant control, sometimes 32-feature edits still failed, and edit magnitude often approached throwing away total weight 1.
rows.uncertainty: The text says statistically significant control; no p-value is stated.
rows.note: This is a limitation on control with these features, not a direct test that the representation is complete.
rows.check: The row omits the frozen-decoder baseline. Frozen-at-initialization task SAEs (random decoder directions) perform on par with full-distribution SAEs in control (Appendix Fig 24). This weakens the full-distribution result further.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5.2, lines 830–841; Figures 23–25 and 29: full-distribution edits often require at least 32 features, remove weight approaching 1, and perform on par with frozen-decoder task SAEs.

relationships.condition: GPT-2 Small IOI circuit locations, task-specific and OpenWebText SAEs
relationships.reason: Both SAE types yield many high-F1 features for IO, S and Pos attributes, consistent with known head roles (r1, r2). The text adds that supervised dictionaries of about 500 features in 64-dim heads give good reconstructions.
relationships.display_finding: Both SAE types gave many high-F1 features for the IO, S and position attributes, consistent with known head roles. Supervised dictionaries of about 500 features in 64-dim heads also reconstructed well.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Task SAEs, name mover outputs, interpretations at F1 threshold 0.6
source_check.reason: Appendices A.13 and A.16 explicitly report high faithfulness and completeness in this condition (r8). Support concerns task-relative completeness; stability and canonicality remain untested by this experiment.

relationships.condition: Task-specific SAEs on IOI activations (L10H0 queries and circuit cross-sections)
relationships.reason: Several results qualify V5 (r3, r4, r5, r6, r9, r10). The binary Pos attribute splits into at least 10 uninterpretable features, only above-chance stable across seeds and data. Causally relevant S names are occluded by slightly higher-norm IO features, with S features never exceeding 22, and this depends on magnitude. Faithfulness falls at F1 0.7 and 0.8. Edits need more features and larger magnitude than supervised edits.
relationships.display_finding: The binary Pos attribute split into at least 10 uninterpretable features that were only above-chance stable across seeds and data, causally relevant S-name features were occluded by slightly higher-norm IO features, faithfulness fell at F1 0.7 and 0.8, and edits needed more features and larger magnitudes than supervised edits.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Task-specific SAEs on IOI activations (L10H0 queries and circuit cross-sections)
source_check.reason: Over-splitting, incomplete recovery of causally relevant S features, magnitude-dependent recovery, threshold-sensitive faithfulness and weaker control qualify dictionary completeness and reliability (r3–r6, r9–r10).

relationships.reason: Statistically significant control often needs 32 or more features, sometimes fails at 32, and edits remove weight approaching 1. Performance is on par with random frozen-decoder SAEs (r11, text Fig 24).
relationships.display_finding: Significant control often needed 32 or more features, sometimes failed at 32, removed weight approaching 1, and performed on par with SAEs using random frozen decoders.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: Control often requires at least 32 features and large edits, sometimes fails at 32, and is comparable to frozen-decoder task SAEs. These findings qualify usefulness as task units without establishing universal absence of meaningful features (r11).

relationships.condition: Toy SAE on a two-Gaussian mixture (d=100, m=1000)
relationships.reason: A randomized many-feature SAE matches or beats the ideal 2-feature decomposition at every lambda tested, and trained SAEs reliably learn many features. The SAE objective need not recover the natural units (r7).
relationships.display_finding: A randomized many-feature SAE matched or beat the ideal 2-feature decomposition at every λ tested, and trained SAEs reliably learned many features, so the objective need not recover the natural units.

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.condition: Toy SAE on a two-Gaussian mixture (d=100, m=1000)
source_check.reason: The randomized many-feature construction is competitive with or better than the ideal two-feature class across the tested penalties, and trained wide SAEs reliably learn many active features. This supplies a synthetic counterexample to canonical recovery by the SAE objective (r7).

relation.reason: The study directly evaluates sparse feature recovery in GPT-2 Small and tests the completeness and reliability of SAE dictionaries using supervised comparisons and synthetic counterexamples.

tranche.reason: Occlusion, over-splitting, threshold dependence and the Gaussian-mixture counterexample directly qualify V5; these results go beyond evaluating a new SAE method.

source_check.notes: Checks cover the visible content of truncated pack fields. The authors acknowledge that supervised task variables may admit alternative, equally consistent parametrizations; task-relative completeness does not establish canonical units.
